topic: Calibration and correlated errors
stem: An instrument reports radius s = a r + b, where r is the true radius in cm. Exact radius standards {r1} and {r2} cm give readings {s1} and {s2} cm. A hollow cylinder gives outer and inner readings {so} and {si} cm; its exact length is {L} cm and mass {m} g. After calibration, a single common additive reading error of magnitude at most {ds} cm affects BOTH specimen readings in the same direction. There are no other errors. Use first-order maximum uncertainty and π = 3.14.
tasks: Find the maximum percentage uncertainty of that density.
Find the maximum absolute uncertainty of that density.
explanation: Two standards give a={a} and b={b} cm. Thus R={ro}, r={ri} cm and ρ={rho} g/cm³. The common error cancels in R−r. Since R²−r²=(R−r)(R+r), its fractional error is 2δs/[a(R+r)], not the sum of two independent radius errors. Hence the density uncertainty is {err}% or {absrho} g/cm³.
reason: Infer scale and zero calibration, reconstruct annular geometry and distinguish a common error from independent radius errors.

topic: Instrument loading and uncertainty
stem: A voltmeter of resistance {Rv} Ω is connected across an unknown wire. An ideal ammeter upstream reads the combined wire and voltmeter current. The readings are {V} V and {I} A. The wire length is {L} m; its diameter reading is {d} mm with a positive zero error {z} mm. Maximum independent errors are {dv} V in voltage and {di} A in current; all other data are exact. Use π=3.14 and first-order bounds.
tasks: Find the maximum percentage uncertainty of corrected resistivity.
Find the maximum absolute uncertainty of corrected resistivity.
explanation: The wire current is J=I−V/Rv={J} A, so R=V/J={R} Ω and ρ={rho} Ω m. Use R=V/(I−V/Rv) before differentiating: |∂R/∂V|=I/J² and |∂R/∂I|=V/J². Thus δR/R=(IδV+VδI)/(VJ)={rel}%, giving δρ={drho} Ω m. Treating V and J as independent overcounts their shared voltage error.
reason: Correct current loading and diameter zero error; differentiate the corrected expression while preserving the correlation caused by voltage subtraction.

topic: Projectile motion with an impact
stem: A particle is launched from (0,0) with velocity ({ux} i + {uy} j) m/s. It strikes a smooth vertical wall at x={wall} m. The coefficient of restitution for the normal velocity is {e}; tangential velocity is unchanged. Gravity is 10 m/s² downward; the floor is y=0. The wall extends above the impact. Ignore air resistance.
tasks: Find the x-coordinate at which it first reaches the floor after impact.
Find its speed just before that floor impact.
Extend the same post-wall trajectory mathematically to x=0. Find its y-coordinate there (a negative value means the actual floor intercept happened earlier).
explanation: At the wall t={t} s, y={y} m and vy={vy} m/s. The impact changes vx to −e ux only. The positive root of y+vy τ−5τ²=0 is τ={flight} s. This gives floor coordinate {land} m and speed {speed} m/s. The x=0 extrapolation uses τ=wall/(e ux), giving y={returnheight} m; it is not an extra physical flight through the floor.
reason: Separate two ballistic stages, apply restitution only to the normal component, select the physical landing root and interpret a boundary crossing.

topic: Delayed pursuit with a speed limit
stem: Car A passes x=0 at t=0 with constant speed {v} m/s. Car B starts from rest at x=0 at t={delay} s, accelerates at {a} m/s² until reaching its speed limit {w} m/s, and then travels at that limit. Both move in +x. Find the first catch after B starts. The stated data do not permit a catch during acceleration.
tasks: Find the clock time of the catch.
Find the catch position measured from x=0.
Find the maximum separation A minus B before the catch.
explanation: B reaches its limit after {ta} s at x={xb} m; the gap then is {gap} m. It takes {coast} s to close at w−v. Thus tcatch={catch} s and xcatch={position} m. The gap first grows and then shrinks: its maximum occurs when B reaches speed v, at elapsed B-time v/a, and equals {separation} m.
reason: Use separate clocks and acceleration/coasting regimes; maximise relative separation at equal speeds rather than at the regime boundary.

topic: Static friction and coupled blocks
stem: A block of mass {m} kg rests on a block of mass {M} kg on a smooth horizontal floor. The upper/lower static and kinetic friction coefficients are {us} and {uk}. A horizontal force {F} N is applied to the LOWER block from rest. Take g=10 m/s². The applied force is above the threshold for slip. The blocks remain in contact horizontally for the time {t} s.
tasks: Find the lower block’s displacement relative to the upper block after that time.
Find the thermal energy generated at the interface over that time.
Find the lower-to-upper kinetic-energy ratio at that time.
explanation: Sticking would require friction mF/(m+M); its limiting force is {limit} N. Since F exceeds that, use kinetic friction. The accelerations are au={au} and al={al} m/s². Relative sliding distance is {relative} m, heat is friction times that distance, {heat} J. The kinetic-energy ratio is M al²/(m au²)={ratio}. Frictional heat is not friction times either individual ground displacement.
reason: Test sticking, switch to kinetic friction, solve two accelerations and distinguish relative sliding work from ground-frame work.

topic: Accelerated support and friction
stem: A fixed incline inside an elevator has sinθ={s} and cosθ={c}. A block of mass {m} kg initially rests on it. The elevator accelerates upward at {a} m/s². A force P parallel UP the incline is increased slowly until upward motion is impending. The static and kinetic friction coefficients are {us} and {uk}. P is then held at that threshold while the block slides upward through {d} m relative to the elevator. Take g=10 m/s².
tasks: Find the final speed relative to the elevator.
Find the work done by P in the elevator frame over that motion.
Find the heat produced by sliding friction.
explanation: Effective downward gravity is g+a. Thus N={N} N. At impending upward slip, friction is downward and P={P} N. Once sliding begins, friction falls to μkN, leaving relative acceleration {ar} m/s². Hence speed={speed} m/s, applied-force work={work} J and frictional heat={heat} J.
reason: Resolve effective gravity in a noninertial frame, distinguish impending and sliding friction, then use the appropriate relative-frame work and motion.

topic: Inferring friction from reversed motion
stem: A {m} kg block on a horizontal rough table is connected over a smooth massless pulley to a hanging mass. In one trial a hanging mass {h1} kg descends with acceleration {a1} m/s². In another, a hanging mass {h2} kg is initially pulled upward and, while still moving upward, has downward acceleration {a2} m/s². The same kinetic friction coefficient applies. An additional hanging mass {h3} kg is then used and moves downward from rest. Take g=10 m/s².
tasks: Find the tension in the third trial.
Find the time to descend 2 m in the third trial.
Find the heat generated in the third trial over a 2 m descent.
explanation: For downward motion, (m+h1)a1=h1g−μmg. During upward motion, friction reverses, so (m+h2)a2=h2g+μmg. Both give μ={mu}. With h3, a={acc} m/s² and T=h3(g−a)={T} N. The two-metre descent takes {time} s and generates {work} J of heat.
reason: Infer friction with a direction reversal, distinguish acceleration from velocity, and solve the new coupled system.

topic: Inelastic impact and a vertical spring
stem: A block of mass {M} kg hangs at rest from a vertical spring of stiffness {k} N/m. A projectile of mass {m} kg moving vertically downward embeds in the block with speed {u} m/s. The impact is brief. Thereafter the spring is lossless and gravity is 10 m/s². Measure subsequent downward displacement from the PRE-IMPACT equilibrium.
tasks: Find the greatest subsequent downward displacement.
Find the greatest spring tension after impact.
Find the work done by gravity from just after impact to the lowest subsequent position.
explanation: During impact momentum gives v={v} m/s. The added mass shifts equilibrium down by δ={delta} m. The post-impact SHM has ω={omega} rad/s and amplitude A=√[δ²+(v/ω)²]={A} m about the NEW equilibrium. Thus the maximum displacement from the old position is {maxdown} m and maximum tension {maxforce} N. The subsequent gravitational work is (M+m)g times this displacement, {gravwork} J.
reason: Separate impulse from subsequent energy, account for the equilibrium shift, and keep the reference position and impact loss distinct.

topic: Spring impact, friction and return motion
stem: A block of mass {m} kg approaches an initially uncompressed spring with speed {u} m/s on a horizontal rough track. The spring constant is {k} N/m and the kinetic friction coefficient is {mu}; take g=10 m/s². The block is not attached to the spring. It compresses the spring, reverses and leaves it; assume the maximum static friction coefficient also equals {mu}.
tasks: Find the speed when the block returns to the spring’s natural length.
Find the distance travelled after leaving the spring until it next stops.
Find the heat generated during the entire contact with the spring.
explanation: During compression the energy equation is kx²/2+fx=mu²/2. Its positive solution is x={x} m. Here kx>f, so reversal occurs; the return energy is kx²/2−fx. The exit speed is {exit} m/s, the later stopping distance {after} m and contact heat 2fx={loss} J.
reason: Solve a quadratic energy balance, verify reversal against static friction, reverse the friction work sign relative to displacement and separate contact from free sliding.

topic: Two-dimensional elastic collision
stem: A particle of mass {m} kg moving along +x at {u} m/s collides elastically with an identical particle initially at rest on a smooth plane. After collision the incident particle travels at angle {theta}° to +x with positive x- and y-components. The initially stationary particle then climbs a smooth incline whose direction is aligned with its outgoing horizontal velocity. Take g=10 m/s².
tasks: Find the greatest height reached by the second particle.
Find the magnitude of the impulse on the incident particle.
Find the second-to-first kinetic-energy ratio immediately after collision.
explanation: Momentum and kinetic energy imply v1·v2=0 for equal masses with one initially at rest. Resolve the incident velocity along the two perpendicular outgoing directions: v1={v1}, v2={v2} m/s. The second particle rises by v2²/(2g)={height} m. The impulse magnitude equals its acquired momentum, {impulse} N s, and the energy ratio is {ratio}.
reason: Combine vector momentum with elastic energy to infer orthogonal velocities, then connect collision outcomes to a climb or impulse.

topic: Angular impact followed by a gravitational swing
stem: A uniform rod of mass {M} kg and length {L} m hangs vertically from a frictionless pivot at its upper end. A projectile of mass {m} kg moving horizontally at {u} m/s embeds at the lower end. The rod-projectile system then swings without loss. Take g=10 m/s². The maximum angle is less than 90° from the initial downward vertical.
tasks: Find the energy dissipated in embedding.
Find the magnitude of the horizontal impulse supplied by the pivot during impact.
explanation: Conserve angular momentum about the pivot, not total horizontal momentum: I={I} kg m², ω={w} rad/s. The post-impact energy is {K} J and equals gL(M/2+m)(1−cosθ), giving θ={angle}°. Embedding loss is {loss} J. The final horizontal momentum is (M/2+m)Lω; its deficit relative to mu is the pivot impulse magnitude {pivot} N s.
reason: Use pivot angular momentum through a nonconservative impact, distributed gravitational potential during the swing, and centre-of-mass momentum for the support impulse.

topic: Recovering inertia from redistribution
stem: A horizontal turntable with unknown fixed moment of inertia I carries two identical point masses, each {m} kg. They are initially at radius {r1} m when its angular speed is {w1} rad/s. They move radially to {r2} m, giving angular speed {w2} rad/s. There is no external torque. They next move to radius {r3} m, with negligible radial kinetic energy at each endpoint.
tasks: Find the final angular speed at the third radius.
Find the net work supplied internally in the second redistribution (negative if energy is extracted).
Find the inward force needed to hold EACH point mass at the third radius once redistribution has ended.
explanation: Conservation between the first two states gives I={I} kg m² and angular momentum H={H} kg m²/s. At r3, ω=H/(I+2mr3²)={w3} rad/s. Internal work is the rotational-energy change at constant H, {work} J. Once the masses are fixed radially, each needs mω²r3={force} N inward.
reason: Infer the unmeasured apparatus inertia from two angular-momentum states, then evaluate a third state and the sign of internal work.

topic: Free rod collision with restitution
stem: A point particle of mass {m} kg moves perpendicular to a uniform rod of mass {M} kg and length {L} m, striking one end. The rod is initially at rest on a smooth horizontal plane. The normal coefficient of restitution is {e}; the particle arrives at {u} m/s. The impact direction is perpendicular to the rod and all impulses lie along it.
tasks: Find the rod’s angular speed immediately after impact.
Find the particle’s signed outgoing velocity along its initial direction.
Find the total kinetic energy lost in impact.
explanation: An impulse J gives rod COM speed J/M and ω=6J/(ML), so the struck end moves at 4J/M. Restitution is 4J/M−(u−J/m)=eu, giving J={J} N s. Thus ω={w} rad/s and particle velocity {v} m/s. Include both rod translation and rotation: rod energy={K} J and total loss={loss} J.
reason: Apply restitution at the moving contact point, couple linear and angular impulses and account for both kinds of rod kinetic energy.

topic: Inverse-square field inferred from two heights
stem: For a spherical nonrotating planet, the gravitational accelerations at heights {h1} m and {h2} m above its surface are {g1} and {g2} m/s². Use Newtonian gravity and ignore atmosphere. A small satellite has a circular orbit at height {h3} m.
tasks: Find the external work per unit mass to move slowly from height h1 to h2.
explanation: The field ratio gives (R+h2)/(R+h1)=√(g1/g2), hence R={r} m and GM={gm} m³/s². Use that inferred radius and gravitational parameter: escape speed={escape} m/s, orbit period={period} s, and potential increase per mass={delta} J/kg. Heights must not be substituted as distances from the centre.
reason: Recover both radius and gravitational parameter from two elevated field measurements, then use potential energy or circular dynamics.

topic: Energy and angular momentum at orbital turning points
stem: A satellite is in a circular orbit of radius {r} m about a pointlike central body with GM={gm} m³/s². An instantaneous tangential impulse changes its speed to {f} times the original circular speed without changing radius. Here 1<f<√2. Afterwards only gravity acts. The impulse point is the orbit’s nearest point; at the farthest point velocity is again tangential.
tasks: Find the greatest distance from the centre reached after the impulse.
Find the satellite’s speed at that farthest point.
Find the decrease in speed between the impulse point and the farthest point on the new orbit.
explanation: Immediately after the impulse, specific energy is ε=GM(f²/2−1)/r and specific angular momentum is h=f√(GM r). At any turning radius x, ε=h²/(2x²)−GM/x. The two roots are r and r f²/(2−f²)={far} m. Then vfar=h/rfar={vf} m/s. Compared with the post-impulse speed f√(GM/r), the decrease is {slowdown} m/s.
reason: Use two conserved quantities to distinguish two radial turning points after a velocity change and connect impulse work to the initial circular state.

topic: Inverse calorimetry with a phase threshold
stem: An insulated calorimeter of unknown heat capacity C contains {mw} kg water at 20°C. Adding {ms} kg of a solid at 100°C produces equilibrium at {T1}°C. In a second trial the same calorimeter instead contains {mw2} kg water at 20°C; adding {ms2} kg of the same solid at 100°C gives {T2}°C. No phase change occurs in these trials. Water specific heat is 4200 J/(kg K). For the fresh trial, remove the solid and replace the water with a fresh {mw} kg charge, equal to the first trial water mass. The calorimeter and this fresh water start at {hot}°C and {ice} kg ice at 0°C is added. Latent heat is 336000 J/kg.
tasks: All added ice melts. Find the final temperature in the fresh ice trial.
Find the largest ice mass at 0°C that could just melt in the fresh system at its stated initial temperature.
After the stated ice trial, find the extra heat needed to raise the complete water-calorimeter system by 10 K.
explanation: The two different water masses give C+mw cw=P cs and C+mw2 cw=Q cs, where P and Q follow from the measured temperature changes. Subtract to obtain the solid specific heat and then H=C+mw cw={H} J/K. Then C={C} J/K and cs={cs} J/(kg K). The available heat at 0°C is {available} J. After melting, Tf={Tf}°C; the just-melting ice mass is {maxice} kg and the subsequent 10 K heat is {extra} J.
reason: Solve two independent mixing constraints for two thermal properties, then check a latent-heat threshold and the changed final heat capacity.

topic: Continuity, Bernoulli and a side pressure tap
stem: Water of density 1000 kg/m³ flows steadily from section 1 of area {A1} cm² to section 2 of area {A2} cm² situated {h} m higher. The measured pressure difference p1−p2 is {dp} Pa. Ignore viscosity and take g=10 m/s². A third section at the height of section 1 has area {A3} cm². Its pressure is p3.
tasks: Find the net rate of pressure work on water between sections 1 and 2.
Find the rate of increase of gravitational potential energy between sections 1 and 2.
explanation: Continuity gives v2/v1=A1/A2. Bernoulli requires dp=ρg h+ρ(v2²−v1²)/2. Thus v1={v1} m/s and Q={Q} m³/s. At section 3, v3={v3} m/s, giving p1−p3={drop} Pa. Pressure-work power is dp Q={power} W; only {rise} W becomes gravitational potential energy, the rest becomes kinetic energy.
reason: Separate pressure work into elevation and kinetic terms, infer flow from an inclined measurement and predict a third section.

topic: Thermal expansion under an internal constraint
stem: Two straight rods have the same original length {L} m and are fastened side by side between two light rigid end plates. The plates can move freely axially and apply no net external force; they remain parallel. The rods share the same extension. Rod 1 has area {A1} mm², Young modulus {Y1} GPa and expansion coefficient {al1}×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹. Rod 2 has corresponding values {A2}, {Y2}, {al2}. Initially both are unstressed. Temperature rises by {DT} K. Use linear elasticity and small expansion.
tasks: Find the magnitude of the axial force in rod 1.
Find the total elastic strain energy in both rods.
explanation: Equal total strain ε and zero net axial force give A1Y1(ε−α1ΔT)+A2Y2(ε−α2ΔT)=0. Hence ε={strain}, extension={extension} mm and rod-1 tensile force={force} N, balanced by rod-2 compression. Elastic energy uses the mechanical strain, not total thermal extension, and is {energy} J.
reason: Couple compatibility and internal force balance, distinguish thermal from elastic strain and sum energy in both materials.

topic: Inferring a thermodynamic path
stem: One mole of an ideal gas has constant Cv={cv}R. In a reversible process pV^n is constant, with unknown n. Its temperature increases from {T1} K to {T2} K while the gas does {W} J of work. Use R=8 J/(mol K). Starting from that final state, the gas is returned to T1 by reversible adiabatic expansion.
tasks: Find the final-to-original volume ratio after both processes.
Find the final-to-original pressure ratio after both processes.
Find the net work done by the gas over the two processes.
explanation: Integrating pV^n=constant gives W=R(T2−T1)/(1−n), hence n={n}. The first volume factor is {vfirst}. For the adiabatic return γ=1+1/Cv(in R units), so its volume factor is {vsecond}. The total factor is {vtotal}. At the restored temperature the pressure ratio is {ptotal}. Adiabatic work equals Cv(T2−T1), so net work is {net} J.
reason: Infer the path exponent from a work measurement, combine two different thermodynamic laws and track signs through an adiabatic return.

topic: Coupled reversible heat engines
stem: Two reversible engines operate in cascade from {Th} K through an unknown intermediate temperature T to {Tc} K. All heat rejected by the first engine enters the second. The first absorbs {Q} J per cycle and delivers {ratio} times the work of the second. A refrigerator working reversibly between Tc and T is later driven by the second engine’s entire work per cycle.
tasks: Find the heat discharged by the driven refrigerator to its hot reservoir per cycle.
Find W1 divided by the sum of the first engine’s heat input and the refrigerator’s hot-reservoir discharge.
explanation: W1=Q(1−T/Th), W2=Q(T−Tc)/Th. The measured work ratio gives T={T} K, W1={W1} J and W2={W2} J. The refrigerator has COP=Tc/(T−Tc), so it extracts {Qc} J and discharges {reject} J. The explicitly requested ratio is {fraction}; it is not a thermal efficiency of an isolated engine.
reason: Use coupled heat flow and a work ratio to infer the middle reservoir, then reverse the thermodynamic device and distinguish heat extracted from heat discharged.

topic: Mixture composition from heat and mass
stem: A mixture contains a monatomic gas of molar mass 4 g/mol and a rigid diatomic gas of molar mass 28 g/mol. The total mass is {mass} g. Heating at constant volume through {dt} K requires {Q} J. Use R=8 J/(mol K). Initially both gases are at {T} K. No rotational modes freeze out and vibration is inactive. The mixture is then reversibly compressed adiabatically to half its volume.
tasks: Find the final rms speed of the diatomic molecules.
Find the work done ON the mixture during compression.
explanation: Mass gives 4a+28b=mass; constant-volume heat gives (12a+20b)ΔT=Q. Thus a={a}, b={b} mol, Cv={Cv} J/K and γ={gamma}. Adiabatic compression gives Tf={Tf} K. Use the diatomic molar mass, not the mixture average, for vrms={vrms} m/s. Work on the gas equals the internal-energy increase, {workon} J.
reason: Infer two gas amounts from independent mass and thermal measurements, form the mixture heat-capacity ratio and apply species-specific kinetic theory after compression.

topic: Kinetic theory with a selective change
stem: A rigid insulated vessel contains {a} mol monatomic gas and {b} mol rigid diatomic gas at {T} K. Through controlled valves, half the monatomic molecules and one quarter of the diatomic molecules are removed slowly while a heater holds temperature at T. After the valves close, {Q} J of heat is supplied at constant volume. Use R=8 J/(mol K); there is no chemical reaction or further particle loss.
tasks: Find the fraction of the final internal energy belonging to the diatomic gas.
If the remaining mixture were instead heated from T to the same final temperature at constant pressure, find the required heat.
explanation: The controlled removal leaves af={af}, bf={bf} mol. Its total Cv={Cv} J/K gives Tf={Tf} K. Pressure depends on both retained mole count and changed temperature: ratio={pressure}. The diatomic internal-energy fraction is {energyfraction}. For the counterfactual constant-pressure heating, Cp=Cv+nR, giving heat={reversible} J.
reason: Track species-selective particle loss, recompute the heat capacity rather than reusing the original mixture, and distinguish particle fraction from energy fraction.

topic: Successive turning points with dry friction
stem: A block of mass {m} kg is attached to a spring of stiffness {k} N/m on a horizontal rough surface. Kinetic and maximum static friction both have magnitude {F} N. At x={A} m to the right of the unstretched position, the block is released from rest. The supplied values guarantee crossings of x=0 on both the first and second traversals. Use Coulomb friction, not viscous damping.
tasks: Find the coordinate of the first right-hand turning point AFTER the first left-hand turning point.
Find the speed at the second crossing of x=0.
Find the total frictional heat by the first return to a right-hand turning point.
explanation: For a half-cycle from +A to −B, k(A²−B²)/2=F(A+B), so B=A−2F/k={left} m. Both spring forces exceed static friction at the necessary reversals. The next right amplitude is B−2F/k={right} m. On the second centre crossing the energy is kB²/2−FB, giving speed {v2} m/s. Total dissipated energy is {heat} J.
reason: Resolve the direction-dependent work over successive half-cycles and test whether a turning point permits another reversal.

topic: Inferring effective gravity and changing the support
stem: A small-angle pendulum of length {L} m is in a vehicle with constant unknown horizontal acceleration a and unknown upward acceleration b. Its equilibrium string makes angle θ with the downward vertical, where sinθ={s}, cosθ={c}. Its measured small-oscillation period is {T} s. Take g=10 m/s². The vehicle’s upward acceleration is then set to zero while its horizontal acceleration remains a.
tasks: Find the small-oscillation period about the NEW equilibrium.
Find the new equilibrium angle from the downward vertical.
Find the new-to-old equilibrium tension ratio for the same bob.
explanation: The measured period fixes ge=4π²L/T²={ge} m/s². Components give a={a} and b={b} m/s² (negative b denotes downward acceleration). Once b is set to zero, effective gravity is √(g²+a²)={newg} m/s². Thus the new period is {newT} s, angle {newangle}° and equilibrium tension ratio {ratio}.
reason: Recover an acceleration vector from a period and tilt measurement, then recompute the equilibrium after changing only one component.

topic: Charge conservation across a switched network
stem: Capacitors C1={C1} μF and C2={C2} μF are separately charged to {V1} V and {V2} V and disconnected from their batteries. They are then joined in parallel with like-sign plates together and allowed to settle through small resistance. The wires are then removed. A dielectric of constant {K} is inserted fully into C1 while it remains isolated. C2 remains unchanged. Finally the two capacitors are again connected with like-sign plates together and allowed to settle. Ignore fringing and leakage.
tasks: Find the heat generated in the SECOND reconnection only.
Find the magnitude of charge entering C1’s originally positive plate during the second reconnection.
explanation: First charge sharing gives V={V} V. Isolated dielectric insertion keeps C1 charge fixed, so its voltage becomes V/K and energy becomes C1 V²/(2K). The second reconnection preserves total plate charge, giving Vf={Vf} V. Its separate energy loss is {loss2} J and C1 gains {transfer} μC. Work during the dielectric step is {work} J and must not be counted as reconnection heat.
reason: Track which charge and voltage remain fixed through three different connection states and separate dielectric work from each dissipative redistribution.

topic: Inferring charges from a null and a potential
stem: Two fixed positive charges are on the x-axis at x=0 and x={d} m. The electric field vanishes at x={x} m between them. The potential at that point is {V} V with zero at infinity. Use k=9×10⁹ N m²/C². A particle of charge {q} μC and mass {m} kg is moved slowly from x={r1} m to x={r2} m, both to the right of the charges.
tasks: Find the external work for the specified slow transfer.
Find the electric-field magnitude at the final position.
In a separate trial released from rest at r1, find the speed at r2 under electric force alone.
explanation: Field cancellation yields Q2/Q1={ratio}. The measured potential then gives Q1={Q} C. At r1 and r2, potentials are {p1} and {p2} V. Slow external work is q(V2−V1)={work} J. Field magnitudes add on the right, giving {field} N/C. In the free trial, the potential decrease gives speed {speed} m/s.
reason: Infer two source charges from different observables, use signed potential work and distinguish quasistatic transport from release dynamics.

topic: Dipole orientation from two energy measurements
stem: A rigid dipole in a uniform electric field has unknown pE and initial angle θ with 0<θ<90°. The slow external work to rotate it from θ to 90° is {W} J. In a separate trial it is released from rest at θ; at first alignment its rotational kinetic energy is {K} J. Its moment of inertia is {I} kg m². Ignore damping. In a third trial it starts from rest at 90° in the same field.
tasks: Find the initial electric-torque magnitude at θ.
Find the angular speed when the third trial first passes 45° to the field.
Find the small-angle oscillation period about stable alignment.
explanation: The slow work is pE cosθ=W; the release energy is pE(1−cosθ)=K. Hence pE={pE} J and θ={theta}°. Torque is √[(pE)²−W²]={torque} N m. From 90° to 45°, energy released is pE cos45°, giving {speed45} rad/s. Near alignment, Iθ̈=−pEθ, giving small-angle period {period} s.
reason: Combine two distinct energy experiments to infer the dipole scale and orientation, then use torque or a separately specified dynamical regime.

topic: Source inference with finite voltmeters
stem: A source has unknown emf E and internal resistance r. A voltmeter of resistance {R1} Ω reads {V1} V when connected alone across it. A second voltmeter of resistance {R2} Ω reads {V2} V when connected alone. Both voltmeters and an external resistor {load} Ω are now connected simultaneously in parallel across the source. All resistances are constant.
tasks: Find the common voltmeter reading with all three branches connected.
Find the power dissipated in the external resistor.
Find the power dissipated inside the source.
explanation: Each reading obeys E=Vi(1+r/Ri). Solving the two equations gives r={r} Ω and E={E} V. The three loads have parallel resistance {Rp} Ω. Their common voltage is {V} V. External resistor power is {power} W, whereas source internal heating uses the total current and is {loss} W.
reason: Recover source parameters from two loading measurements, then solve a new parallel loading condition without treating the meters as ideal.

topic: Metre bridge with end correction
stem: A uniform 100 cm bridge wire has total resistance {Rw} Ω. A contact resistance e occurs only at its LEFT end before the uniform wire begins. With resistance X in the left gap and {R} Ω in the right gap, balance occurs at {l1} cm from the left end of the uniform wire. When the gap resistances are interchanged, balance occurs at {l2} cm. The contact resistance stays at the same physical end. The uniform wire temperature and e are unchanged.
tasks: If the left contact resistance is removed, find the shift of the ORIGINAL balance point (positive to the right).
Find the equivalent resistance of X and R connected in parallel outside the bridge.
explanation: The two ratios are X/R=(e+Rw l1/100)/[Rw(100−l1)/100] and its reciprocal with l2. Multiplying produces e²+B e+C=0. The nonnegative root gives e={e} Ω and X={X} Ω. With e removed the original connection balances at {ideal} cm, a shift {shift} cm. The separate parallel combination is {parallel} Ω.
reason: Keep the parasitic resistance at its physical end while swapping arms, solve the nonlinear pair of balance conditions and predict the corrected bridge.

topic: Helical trajectory inferred from geometry
stem: An ideal nonrelativistic positively charged particle is accelerated from rest through {V} V and enters a uniform magnetic field {B} T at an unknown angle. Its helical radius is {r} m and its advance parallel to the field per turn is {p} m. No electric field acts in this region. For a separate second trial, the particle is first brought to rest and then accelerated through {V2} V and enters a second magnetic region of field {B2} T at the SAME angle.
tasks: Find the gyroperiod in the second region.
Find the actual distance travelled in one turn in the second region.
Find the helical pitch in the second region.
explanation: Geometry gives cotθ=p/(2πr)={slope}. Since v⊥=(q/m)Br and v²=2(q/m)V, q/m={qm} C/kg. The second speed is {speed} m/s and period {period} s. Actual path per turn is vT={path} m; only the parallel component produces pitch, {pitch} m.
reason: Infer launch angle and charge-to-mass ratio from helical geometry and acceleration energy, then transfer both to a changed voltage and field.

topic: Torsional equilibrium with magnetic torque
stem: A coil of unknown magnetic moment magnitude μ is suspended on a linear torsion fibre of unknown torsion constant κ. Its untwisted normal is perpendicular to a uniform field. In field {B1} T it turns through {th1} radians toward alignment. A separate mechanical calibration with the field off stores {U} J in the fibre at twist {cal} radians. Use the exact sine/cosine torque law, not the small-angle approximation.
tasks: Find the field magnitude that would give equilibrium at twice the original twist.
At the ORIGINAL field B1, find the quasistatic external work to move from untwisted to twice the original twist.
At the original field B1 and twice the original twist, find the signed net torque, positive toward increasing twist.
explanation: The mechanical calibration gives κ={k} N m/rad. Equilibrium requires κθ=μB cosθ, yielding μ={mu} A m². At twice the twist equilibrium requires B2={B2} T. In the original field, total potential is κφ²/2−μB1 sinφ, so external work is {work} J and net torque μB1 cosφ−κφ is {moment} N m.
reason: Combine a mechanical energy calibration and nonlinear magnetic equilibrium, then distinguish a changed-field equilibrium from forced rotation in the original field.

topic: Motional induction with mechanical friction
stem: A conducting rod of length {L} m moves on horizontal rails in an unknown uniform perpendicular field B. The circuit resistance is {R} Ω. Mechanical kinetic friction has an unknown constant magnitude f. A horizontal force {F1} N gives terminal speed {v1} m/s; a second force {F2} N gives terminal speed {v2} m/s in the same direction. Self-inductance is negligible. A third force {F3} N is used under unchanged conditions.
tasks: Find the terminal current with the third force.
Find the circuit’s terminal Joule-heating power with the third force.
Find the charge crossing a circuit section during a further 3 m displacement after terminal motion has been reached.
explanation: At terminal speed F=f+(B²L²/R)v. The two trials give drag coefficient {drag} N s/m and f={fr} N, hence B={B} T. With F3, v={v3} m/s, current={current} A and Joule heat rate={power} W. Charge over distance d follows ∫I dt=BLd/R, giving {charge} C; mechanical frictional heat is separate.
reason: Infer magnetic drag and mechanical friction from two terminal states, recover the field, and distinguish circuit dissipation from total applied power.

topic: Inferring RLC parameters from phase measurements
stem: An ideal series RLC circuit is driven by a fixed RMS voltage {V} V. At angular frequency {w} rad/s its current is {I} A and lags voltage by 45°. At half that angular frequency its current is again I but leads by 45°. All component values remain fixed. The supply frequency is then set to resonance.
tasks: Find the RMS capacitor voltage at resonance.
Find the maximum capacitor energy during resonance.
explanation: At the first frequency ωL−1/(ωC)=R; at ω/2 the net reactance is −R. The magnitude gives R={R} Ω. Solving the signed equations gives L={L} H and C={C} F. Resonance is ω0={wr} rad/s with current {Ir} A. VC,rms={Vc} V. Maximum energy uses peak voltage √2VC, hence C VC,rms²={energy} J.
reason: Use signed phase information at two frequencies to determine separate reactances and distinguish RMS from peak energy at resonance.

topic: Plane-wave energy measured by calorimetry
stem: A small detector has unknown heat capacity C. A heater of resistance {R} Ω carrying {I} A for {t} s raises it by {dT} K. After cooling, a plane electromagnetic wave illuminates a detector area {A} cm² for {time} s and raises it by {rise} K. The face normal makes {theta}° with the propagation direction; a fraction {absorb} of the intercepted energy is absorbed. Ignore losses. Use ε0=8.85×10⁻¹² F/m, c=3×10⁸ m/s and photon energy hc/λ with h=6.63×10⁻³⁴ J s and λ={lam} nm.
tasks: Find the peak electric-field magnitude of the wave.
Find the mean number of photons absorbed per second.
explanation: Electrical calibration gives C={C} J/K. The optical absorbed power is {power} W. Correct both projected area and absorption to get intensity {intensity} W/m². Mean intensity is ε0 c E0²/2, so E0={E} V/m and B0={B} T. Absorbed photons per second equal absorbed power divided by hc/λ, {photons} s⁻¹.
reason: Combine electrical calibration, thermal energy, oblique interception and peak-versus-average wave energy before finding fields or photon counts.

topic: A plane wave and a loaded photoelectric detector
stem: A monochromatic plane wave has peak electric field {E} V/m and frequency {freq} Hz. It is normally incident on a detector of area {A} cm². A fraction {reflect} is reflected; of the absorbed photons, {yieldq} produce one collected electron each. The photocurrent charges an initially uncharged capacitor {C} μF for {t} s; an ideal collection arrangement maintains that constant current. Take ε0=8.85×10⁻¹² F/m, c=3×10⁸ m/s, h=6.63×10⁻³⁴ J s and e=1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C.
tasks: Find the capacitor voltage after the stated time.
Find the stored capacitor energy then.
Find stored capacitor energy divided by optical energy absorbed over that time.
explanation: Use mean rather than peak wave energy density. Absorbed power is {power} W and current is {current} A. Charge It gives voltage {V} V and capacitor energy {energy} J. The requested energy ratio is {ratio}. The specified ideal collection arrangement is part of the model; no claim is made that a passive solar cell holds constant current at arbitrary voltage.
reason: Connect peak field, photon flux, reflection and quantum yield to a changing electrical storage state.

topic: Two lenses with a virtual intermediate object
stem: A converging lens L1 forms a real image of an object {u} cm to its left. The image is {v} cm to its right. A second thin converging lens L2 is placed {d} cm to the right of L1, before that first image would form (d<v). With both lenses present the final image is {z} cm to the right of L2. The object is then moved to {u2} cm to the left of L1, with both lenses fixed.
tasks: Find the final image distance to the right of L2 for the moved object.
Find the SIGNED overall transverse magnification for the moved object.
Find the distance from the moved object to its final image.
explanation: L1 has f1={f1} cm. In the calibration, L2 sees a virtual object v−d cm to its right, so 1/f2=1/z−1/(v−d), giving f2={f2} cm. For the moved object L1 alone would image at {v1new} cm; the signed real-object distance at L2 is {u2lens} cm. The final image is {final} cm beyond L2, signed magnification {mag}, and object-image distance {distance} cm.
reason: Infer the second lens from a virtual-object calibration, recompute the intermediate image after moving the object and preserve magnification signs.

topic: Interference visibility after attenuation
stem: Two coherent monochromatic beams of identical linear polarisation produce maximum intensity {imax} and minimum intensity {imin} W/m². A filter with intensity transmission {t} is inserted in the initially stronger beam. An additional plate then introduces phase delay {phase}° in that beam. The original phase difference at the observation point was 0°.
tasks: Find the intensity at the specified point with both filter and plate present.
Find the visibility (Imax−Imin)/(Imax+Imin) after the filter is inserted.
Find the filter intensity transmission that would instead make the interference minima exactly dark.
explanation: The original amplitude magnitudes are a={a}, b={b} in square-root intensity units. A transmission t multiplies amplitude by √t, so the filtered amplitude is {af}. Phasor addition gives I={I} W/m² and visibility={visibility}. Exactly dark minima require equal amplitudes, hence transmission (b/a)²={factor}.
reason: Recover separate field amplitudes from two intensity extrema, distinguish amplitude and intensity transmission and impose a destructive-interference condition.

topic: Interference shifts with two different media
stem: In a Young double-slit experiment the slit separation is {d} mm and screen distance is {D} m. The measured fringe width is {beta} mm. A plate of thickness {t} μm is inserted before slit 1 and moves the central maximum by {shift} mm toward slit 1. The plate is then replaced by a stack containing {t2} μm of the same material and {t3} μm of index {n3}; slit 2 remains uncovered. Neglect reflection and use normal incidence. All shifts are small-angle shifts in air.
tasks: Find the central-fringe shift with the replacement stack.
Find that shift in fringe widths.
Find the thickness of index-n3 material needed before slit 2 to restore the central maximum to its original position while the stack stays before slit 1.
explanation: The baseline wavelength is {lam} m. The first shift gives original plate index n={n}. The replacement optical delay is the sum of the two excess optical paths, {delay} m. This gives shift {newshift} mm or {fringes} fringes. Compensation requires equal delay before slit 2, so thickness={comp} μm.
reason: Infer wavelength and plate index from independent observations, add excess optical paths and solve a compensating-path condition.

topic: Photoelectric measurements with a voltage offset
stem: A photoelectric apparatus displays stopping reading S=Kmax/e+δ, where δ is an unknown constant instrumental offset. For photon energies {E1} and {E2} eV the displayed readings are {S1} and {S2} V. An independent calibration shows display δ={offset} V when true voltage is zero. Under illumination with photon energy {E3} eV, emitted electrons are accelerated through a further {Va} V. Use λ(nm)=√[0.0150/K(eV)] for a nonrelativistic electron and hc=1240 eV nm.
tasks: Find the final de Broglie wavelength of the fastest electrons.
Find their final-to-initial speed ratio across the extra accelerating stage.
Find the threshold wavelength of the emitting surface.
explanation: Correct the offset before using Einstein’s equation: work function φ={phi} eV. The second measurement checks the same φ. For E3 the maximum kinetic energy is {K} eV; after extra acceleration it is {final} eV. The final matter wavelength is {wave} nm, speed ratio {ratio}, and optical threshold wavelength {threshold} nm.
reason: Distinguish the measured stopping reading from physical stopping potential, infer work function and transfer photoelectron energy through a second electric stage.

topic: Matter-wave observations and energy selection
stem: Electrons have unknown initial kinetic energy K0. Passing through a retarding potential {V} V increases their de Broglie wavelength by a factor {r}. They remain nonrelativistic and none is turned back. An identical initial electron beam is instead accelerated through {A} V. Use λ(nm)=√[0.0150/K(eV)]. A photon of energy {photon} eV produces the initial electrons as maximum-energy photoelectrons.
tasks: Find the electron wavelength after the accelerating trial.
Find the emitter’s threshold wavelength, using hc=1240 eV nm.
Find the kinetic-energy ratio of the accelerated electrons to the retarded electrons.
explanation: Since wavelength is inverse momentum, Kret=K0/r²=K0−V, so K0={K} eV. The accelerated state has {new} eV and wavelength {wave} nm. Einstein’s equation gives φ={phi} eV and threshold {threshold} nm. The accelerated-to-retarded energy ratio is {ratio}.
reason: Invert a matter-wave ratio under retarding work, select the transmitted regime and connect the recovered energy to a separate acceleration and photoelectric threshold.

topic: Energy partition with a moving centre of mass
stem: A composite nucleus of mass {M}u moves along +x at speed {V} m/s and splits into products of masses {m1}u and {m2}u, where M=m1+m2 to the accuracy used for kinetic energy. The released internal energy is {Q} MeV. In the centre-of-mass frame the lighter product is emitted along +x and the heavier along −x. Use u=1.66×10⁻²⁷ kg and 1 MeV=1.6×10⁻¹³ J; all speeds are nonrelativistic. The small mass defect is included only through Q.
tasks: Find the lighter product’s kinetic energy in the laboratory.
Find the heavier product’s kinetic energy in the laboratory.
Find the rate at which their separation grows immediately after breakup.
explanation: In the COM frame, equal opposite momenta give p={p} kg m/s from Q=p²/(2m1)+p²/(2m2). Add the COM velocity V to each signed product velocity. Laboratory velocities are {v1} and {v2} m/s. Their lab energies are {K1} and {K2} MeV and separation speed is {relative} m/s. The lab energies do not divide Q in the inverse-mass ratio.
reason: Partition release energy in the centre-of-mass frame, transform signed velocities to the lab and distinguish released energy from total laboratory kinetic energy.

topic: Inferring a hydrogenic state from two observables
stem: For a one-electron ion of unknown nuclear charge Z, the ionisation energy from level n is {ion} eV and the orbital radius at that level is {radius} a0. Use En=−13.6 Z²/n² eV and rn=a0 n²/Z. The ion makes a transition to level {lower}, then absorbs a {photon} eV photon that ionises it. Use hc=1240 eV nm and the nonrelativistic electron relation λ(nm)=√[0.0150/K(eV)].
tasks: Find the wavelength emitted in the downward bound-state transition.
Find the de Broglie wavelength of the photoelectron produced afterwards.
Find the final bound orbit’s radius, before ionisation, in units of a0.
explanation: Multiply the initial radius factor and ionisation energy to obtain Z={Z}; then n={n}. The final bound level has binding {binding} eV and radius {rnew}a0. Transition photon energy is {emitted} eV, giving wavelength {wave} nm. Subsequent excess photon energy gives electron wavelength {ewave} nm.
reason: Infer both atomic charge and state from independent radius and binding measurements, then distinguish a spectral photon from the later matter wave.

topic: Zener regulation inferred from two load regimes
stem: An ideal DC source of unknown voltage Vs supplies a node through an unknown series resistor R. A {Vz} V ideal Zener is reverse-connected from the node to ground. With load {L1} Ω to ground the node reads {U1} V, below breakdown; the Zener carries no current. With load {L2} Ω it regulates at Vz and carries {Iz} A. In a third trial the load is {L3} Ω. Ignore leakage and Zener dynamic resistance; verify the operating state before using Vz.
tasks: Find the smallest load resistance at which the Zener just enters breakdown.
explanation: The first state gives Vs=U1(1+R/L1). The second gives Vs=Vz+R(Vz/L2+Iz). Together R={R} Ω and Vs={Vs} V. The open-Zener divider would give {unreg} V in trial 3. Thus node={node} V and IZ={IZ3} A, with load power={P} W. The transition load is {limit} Ω.
reason: Infer source parameters across two different diode regimes, test a third regime and solve the load threshold rather than assuming regulation.

topic: Piecewise diode clipping with a finite source
stem: A source of unknown emf E feeds node X through an unknown series resistor R. A load {L} Ω connects X to ground. Two ideal diodes connect X to ideal reference nodes: the upper diode conducts from X into +{upper} V, and the lower from +{lower} V into X. Both are off in a calibration when an adjustable source replaces E: source voltage {S1} V gives X={X1} V, while source voltage {S2} V gives X={X2} V. After calibration the source is fixed at {E} V. The reference supplies can absorb or deliver current as necessary.
tasks: Find the current entering the upper reference through its diode.
Find the series resistor’s power dissipation at the fixed source voltage.
Find the source voltage below which the lower diode begins to conduct as the adjustable source is reduced.
explanation: Off-state calibration gives R={R} Ω; the second point checks the same divider. At fixed E the unclipped node is {free} V. Testing the two inequalities gives X={X} V. Upper-reference current follows node balance, {Iupper} A, and the source resistor dissipates {power} W. The lower transition occurs when the off-state divider reaches the lower reference, at {threshold} V.
reason: Infer the source resistance from an unclipped regime, test both ideal-diode inequalities and apply current balance in the conducting regime.

topic: Vernier readings and a displaced-volume crosscheck
stem: A vernier has 20 divisions equal to 19 main-scale divisions; one main-scale division is 1 mm. With jaws closed its zero lies to the right and division {zero} coincides. For a solid sphere the main-scale reading is {ms} mm and division {coinc} coincides. The sphere’s mass is {mass} g. The displacement of water measured independently is {vol} cm³. Use π=3.14. Treat the mass and displacement measurement as exact; the corrected diameter has maximum uncertainty one least count.
tasks: Find the maximum absolute density uncertainty from the diameter reading.
If zero correction is omitted, find the signed percentage bias in inferred density relative to the corrected value.
Use the corrected geometric volume, checking it against the independent displacement, to find the sphere density.
explanation: Least count is 1−19/20={lc} mm. Subtract the positive zero error, giving d={d} mm and V={V} cm³, consistent with the stated displacement. Density is {rho} g/cm³. Since ρ∝d⁻³, its first-order percentage bound is {error}% and absolute bound {absolute} g/cm³. Without correction the larger diameter lowers inferred density; signed bias={bias}%.
reason: Derive least count, correct the signed zero error, reconcile an independent volume measurement and propagate a cubic measurement dependence.

topic: Galvanometer calibration and ammeter conversion
stem: A galvanometer in series with {R} Ω across an ideal {E} V source deflects {div} divisions. A shunt of {S} Ω across the galvanometer reduces the deflection to one half, while the same series resistor and source remain connected. Do not assume the series resistance is infinite. The instrument’s full-scale deflection is {fs} divisions. It will be converted to an ammeter with full-scale current {range} A.
tasks: Find the shunt resistance needed for the specified ammeter range.
Find the coil heating power at full-scale ammeter current.
Find the ammeter’s terminal voltage drop at full scale.
explanation: The exact half-deflection equations give G=SR/(R−S)={G} Ω. Current per division is {merit} A/div, so full-scale coil current is {Ifs} A. The ammeter shunt carries range−Ifs, giving {shunt} Ω. Coil power is {power} W and the common coil/shunt voltage is {burden} V.
reason: Use the finite-resistance half-deflection circuit to infer coil resistance and current sensitivity, then design and evaluate an ammeter at a different full-scale current.

topic: Thermal equilibrium followed by adiabatic loading
stem: An ideal monatomic gas under a frictionless piston has initial pressure {p} Pa, volume {V} m³ and temperature {T} K. Heat is supplied quasistatically at constant pressure until the volume doubles. The system is then thermally insulated and compressed quasistatically until the pressure is {factor} times the initial pressure. Use γ=5/3. The gas amount remains fixed and the only mechanical work is p–V work.
tasks: Find the net work done BY the gas across both stages.
Find the total internal-energy increase divided by the heat supplied in the first stage.
explanation: After constant-pressure expansion the state is (p,2V,2T). Adiabatic compression gives Vf={vf} m³ and Tf={tf} K. Its signed work is (p_initial V_initial−p_final V_final)/(γ−1)={w2} J. Adding first-stage work yields {net} J. The supplied heat is {heat} J; the specified internal-energy ratio is {ratio}.
reason: Carry the intermediate state across a change in thermal regime, maintain work signs and reconcile heat with the overall internal-energy change.

topic: Apparent depth with a calibrated microscope
stem: A travelling microscope has an additive vertical-coordinate zero offset. With no slab, a bottom mark reads {b} mm. After a transparent slab is placed over that mark, the slab top reads {top} mm and the apparent mark reads {apparent} mm, with increasing readings upward. All readings share the same zero. Under near-normal viewing, that slab is replaced by a two-layer stack with {t1} mm of the same material and {t2} mm of refractive index {n2}. The bottom mark is fixed and air is above the stack.
tasks: Find the apparent-mark microscope reading with the stack.
Find the effective refractive index inferred by treating the full stack as one uniform slab.
Find the apparent depth of the mark measured downward from the stack’s top.
explanation: Coordinate differences remove the offset. The original real and apparent depths give n={n}. For the stack the apparent depths add: t1/n+t2/n2={depth} mm, so upward shift={shift} mm and reading={reading} mm. The single-slab inferred index is total thickness/apparent depth={effective}; it is not the arithmetic mean of the indices.
reason: Remove a shared coordinate offset, infer an optical material property and combine two apparent depths with a different reference surface.

topic: Resonance readings with a fixed end correction
stem: At air temperature {T1} K, the first two resonance lengths of a closed-end resonance tube are {l1} and {l2} cm with one tuning fork. At {T2} K the first resonance with the SAME fork is {newl} cm. The same end correction e applies in both trials; sound speed is proportional to √T. At T1 an independent sound-speed measurement gives {c1} m/s. Treat air as ideal, with tube dimensions unchanged.
tasks: Find the sound speed in the warm trial, using the resonance readings and the independent T1 speed.
Find the third resonance length at T2.
A second fork has frequency 2f. Find the beat frequency between it and a hypothetical fork whose frequency is 2f/√(T2/T1).
explanation: At T1, λ1=2(l2−l1)={lam1} m and e=(l2−3l1)/2={end} cm. Thus f={f} Hz. The warm first resonance gives λ2=4(newl+e)={lam2} m and c2={speed2} m/s, consistent with √T scaling. The third resonance length is newl+λ2={third} cm. The explicitly specified fork pair produces {beat} Hz beats.
reason: Remove end correction using two modes, preserve the fork frequency across temperature change and distinguish physical tube length from effective resonant length.
